note.explanation: A manometer compares the pressure of a gas with atmospheric pressure. The difference between the mercury levels shows whether the gas pressure is greater or less than atmospheric pressure.
examples: If mercury is lower in the arm connected to the gas, the gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.
If mercury is higher in the arm connected to the gas, the gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
note.checkAnswer: The gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.
note.simple: Think of the two mercury levels as a pressure comparison: the gas pushes mercury down in its arm when its pressure is greater.
note.checkQuestion: A gas is connected to one arm of a manometer. Mercury is lower in that arm than in the open arm. Is the gas pressure greater or less than atmospheric pressure?
note.title: Reading a simple manometer
steps: Check which arm is connected to the gas and which arm is open.
Compare the mercury levels in the two arms.
If mercury is lower in the gas-connected arm, gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.
If mercury is higher in the gas-connected arm, gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
note.answer: A simple manometer compares the pressure of a gas with atmospheric pressure by showing the difference between the mercury levels.

options: The mercury levels in both arms are equal.
Mercury is lower in the open arm.

mcqs.stem: Before a gas cylinder is connected, what happens to the mercury levels in a simple manometer?
rationales: This is correct because atmospheric pressure acts equally at both open ends.
This is wrong because equal atmospheric pressures do not create this level difference.
This is wrong because no gas pressure is acting in one arm yet.
This is wrong because equal pressure keeps the mercury in the tube.

options: The gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.
The gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
The gas pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
The manometer cannot compare the pressures.
mcqs.stem: Mercury is lower in the arm connected to a gas cylinder than in the open arm. What does this indicate?
rationales: This is correct: the gas pushes the mercury down in its arm, showing greater pressure.
This is wrong because a lower mercury level in the gas-connected arm indicates greater, not less, gas pressure.
This is wrong because equal pressures would leave the mercury levels at the same height.
This is wrong because the level difference is used to compare the pressures.

options: The gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.
The gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
The pressure is exactly zero.
The atmospheric pressure is zero.
mcqs.stem: Mercury is higher in the arm connected to the gas than in the open arm. What does this indicate?
rationales: This is wrong because greater gas pressure would push mercury lower in the connected arm.
This is correct: the gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
This is wrong because the mercury level difference does not mean the gas pressure is zero.
This is wrong because the open arm is still subject to atmospheric pressure.

written.text: Describe the working and applications of a simple mercury barometer and a manometer.
written.finalAnswer: A mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure from the height of its mercury column. A manometer compares gas pressure with atmospheric pressure using the difference between mercury levels in its two arms.

modelAnswer: A simple mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure by the height of its mercury column.
A simple manometer consists of a U-shaped glass tube which contains mercury.
One arm is connected to the gas and the other arm is left open to the atmosphere.
The difference between the mercury levels shows whether the unknown gas pressure is greater or less than atmospheric pressure.

examTips: A board question may ask you to describe how a simple manometer works or interpret a diagram.
For full marks, identify the gas-connected and open arms, compare the mercury levels, and state whether gas pressure is greater or less than atmospheric pressure.
If asked why the levels are initially equal, state that atmospheric pressure at the two open ends is the same.

hints: First compare the mercury levels in the two arms.
Mercury is lower in the gas-connected arm, so the gas pushes more strongly than the atmosphere.
yourTurn.question: In Fig. 6.11, the mercury level in the short arm connected to the gas is lower than that in the long open arm. What does this tell you about the unknown pressure?
solution: The short arm is connected to the gas and the long arm is open to the atmosphere.
The mercury level is lower in the arm connected to the gas.
Therefore, the unknown gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.
yourTurn.answer: The unknown gas pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.

hints: Identify which arm is open and which arm is connected to the gas.

yourTurn.question: In Fig. 6.12, the mercury level in the short arm connected to the gas is higher than that in the long open arm. What does this tell you about the unknown pressure?
solution: The short arm is connected to the gas and the long arm is open to the atmosphere.
The mercury level is higher in the arm connected to the gas.
Therefore, the unknown gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.
yourTurn.answer: The unknown gas pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.

explain.title: The manometer
explain.body: A simple manometer consists of a U-shaped glass tube which contains mercury. It compares an unknown gas pressure with atmospheric pressure.

explain.title: Equal starting levels
explain.body: In the beginning, atmospheric pressure at the two open ends of the tube is the same and hence, mercury level in the two arms remains same.

explain.title: Gas pressure greater than atmospheric pressure
explain.body: If the mercury level in the arm connected to the gas is lower than in the open arm, the unknown pressure is more than atmospheric pressure.

explain.title: Gas pressure less than atmospheric pressure
explain.body: If the mercury level in the arm connected to the gas is higher than in the open arm, the unknown pressure is less than atmospheric pressure.

mistakes: Do not confuse which arm is connected to the gas and which is open to the atmosphere.
Do not say gas pressure is greater when mercury is higher in the gas-connected arm; it is lower in that case.
Do not confuse the height difference between mercury levels with the length of the tube.
When explaining the starting levels, mention that atmospheric pressure acts equally at both open ends.
